core.text: Two words make **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudātus est)**: the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised) plus the present of *sum*. *Mārcus pulsātus est* — Marcus was hit. The participle agrees with the subject, so a woman says *pulsāta sum* and several boys *pulsātī sumus*. Latin name: *perfectum indicātīvī passīvī*.
English also builds this with two words, *was* + participle: *the letter was written*, *they have been seen*.
Participle (agreeing with the subject) + sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt. Translate est as 'was' or 'has been', not 'is'.

invented.en: The letter was written by Julius.

core.text: Same tense, opposite direction: **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)** is one word on the perfect stem, *Sextus Mārcum pulsāvit* — Sextus hit Marcus; the passive is participle + *est*: Marcus is the one *ā Sextō pulsātus est* — hit by Sextus. The doer moves into ā / ab + ablative.

teach.title: Two words, one tense

notice.ask: Which two words in each sentence together say 'was shut' and 'were picked'?

teach.say: To say that a thing was done to somebody, Latin writes two words and means one tense: **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudātus est)**. *Puer laudātus est* — the boy was praised. Do not read *est* as a separate 'is': the two words are working together as one verb.

check.ask: Which two words together say 'was praised'?

teach.title: How the pair is built: participle + est
teach.say: Take the perfect participle — the fourth dictionary form used as an adjective — and put the present of *sum* beside it: *clausum* + *est* = *clausum est*, was shut. The participle carries the meaning, *est* carries the person, and in this pair *est* is always 'was' or 'has been'.

check.ask: Fill in the 'he / she / it' cell of the perfect passive.

teach.title: More than one: -ī or -ae, and sunt
teach.say: For more than one, the participle takes a plural ending and *sum* becomes *sunt*: *puerī laudātī sunt*, *rosae carptae sunt*. The participle agrees with whoever the sentence is about, so its ending tells you their gender as well as their number.

check.ask: Fill in the 'they' cell of the perfect passive.

teach.title: Talking about yourself
teach.say: One participle serves every person; only the part of *sum* changes. *vocātus sum*, I was called; *reprehēnsus es*, you were blamed; *vocātī sumus*, we were called; *doctī estis*, you were taught. Six forms of the verb, and the same word doing the work in all six.

check.ask: Fill in 'I was called' and 'you were called'.

teach.title: One word, or two?
teach.say: One word ending in *-tur* is the present passive, happening now: *parātur*, it is being got ready. Two words, participle plus *est*, are the perfect passive, already over: *parātus est*, it has been got ready. Counting the words settles the tense before you translate anything.

check.ask: Which of the two verbs here is passive, and how many words is it?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: The two words may swap places (*scrīpta est* or *est scrīpta*), and other words may stand between them. Whoever did the deed comes in with *ā* or *ab*: *ā nautīs*, *ā patre meō*. Find the participle, find the part of *sum*, and read the two as one verb.

check.ask: *emō, emere, ēmī, ēmptum*. Put 'was bought' in the gap, agreeing with *vīlla*.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) warn that *est* looks present but the tense is past; that oddity comes from the Latin perfect doubling as a simple past. Neuter subjects take -um: *hoc scītum est* — this was known.

Ørberg (cap. XXI) contrasts *pater fīlium laudāvit* with *fīlius laudātus est ā patre*. In the accusative + infinitive the same participle goes with *esse*: *dīcit sē laudātum esse* — he says he was praised.
